state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of it this way: Imagine you have a group of friends and you all go on a hike together. If each person walks twice as fast as before, would the total distance you cover change? Think about how this analogy relates to changing the heights of the plants.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, so if we all walk twice as fast, we'd cover twice the distance... but I'm not really sure how that connects to the plants? Like, is that saying the range would change when we cut the plants in half, or are you saying something else?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine if each person in your group walked at a different speed. Would changing everyone's speed by the same proportion affect how far apart each person is from each other? Think about how this relates to the heights of the plants and whether changing them by the same proportion would impact the range.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses an analogy about walking speed that is mathematically flawed (doubling speed doesn't double distance in a fixed time scenario) and confusing to the student, who shows no improvement and remains uncertain about the core misconception by the end.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use a real-world analogy (hiking with friends), the analogy is confusing and poorly mapped to the mathematical concept—it conflates speed/distance with range, and doesn't clearly connect to how transformations affect the spread of data values.
